previous_admission_summary.summary_paragraph: A 50-year-old man with alcoholic cirrhosis, opioid use disorder, and diastolic heart failure was admitted after being found altered at home following alcohol relapse. He presented with alcohol withdrawal symptoms, abdominal pain, and leg edema. He was managed in the MICU with a phenobarbital taper, thiamine, and multivitamins. Electrolyte abnormalities including hypokalemia and hypophosphatemia were corrected with aggressive repletion. Diuretics were restarted for volume overload due to diastolic heart failure. Iron deficiency anemia was identified and treated with oral iron. He was stabilized, transitioned to oral medications, and discharged home with follow-up plans for his liver, heart, and substance use. He was strongly advised to abstain from alcohol.
problems: Acute on chronic diastolic (congestive) heart failure
Alcoholic cirrhosis of liver without ascites

Brief Hospital Course:
SUMMARY: ___ h/o alcoholic cirrhosis, alcohol use disorder with 
history of complicated withdrawal, opioid use disorder, chronic 
pancreatitis who was admitted for alcohol detox, treated with 
phenobarbital taper, with TTE consistent with hepatopulmonary 
syndrome, treated for hepatic encephalopathy with lactulose and 
rifaximin.

============
ACUTE ISSUES
=============
# EtOH use disorder, c/b acute EtOH withdrawal: Multiple detoxes 
in the past, last drink was ___. On admission, his blood alcohol 
was 309, UTox otherwise negative. He was initially admitted to 
the ICU given his history of complicated withdrawals and 
refeeding syndrome, and underwent phenobarbital loading. He was 
also loaded with thiamine and folate with subsequent daily 
thiamine/folate/multivitamin po and his electrolytes were 
repleted as needed. He was hemodynamically stable but had 
significant anxiety and endorsed intermittent visual symptoms of 
monocular diplopia (as below) and small black dots in the 
corners of his vision. He was transferred to the general 
medicine floor in stable condition and completed his 
phenobarbital taper without issues (last day was ___. For 
his anxiety, he was maintained on prn hydroxyzine and clonidine 
as below. Acamprosate was also discussed and the patient was 
interested in starting, decision deferred to outpatient 
management. He is not a good candidate for naltrexone given his 
liver disease.
[] Social work/addiction nursing following through admission, 
plans for dual diagnosis day program pending at time of 
discharge
[] Consider acamprosate as an outpatient

# EtOH cirrhosis (MELD-Na 17, Child B): No varices on last EGD, 
but some bloody vomit on admission, no further episodes. Stable 
H/H at baseline. INR 1.2. RUQUS showed no ascites. Asterixis 
noted on exam, with mildly altered mental status as compared to 
baseline. Started on lactulose ___, titrated over the course of 
admission to ___ BM's per day with mild improvement in altered 
mental status.
[] Continue Lactulose to 30 mg bid for ___ daily
[] Continue Rifaximin 550 mg po bid
[] 2g sodium diet, 2L fluid restriction
[] Hepatology f/u as scheduled, will need repeat EGD and 
possible transplant eval (HPS)
[] Patient was administered initial doses of HBV/HAV vaccines, 
will need subsequent doses at 1mo/6mo and 6mo respectively; 
unclear if previously immunized w/ PPSV23

# Hepatopulmonary syndrome
# Hypoxia, tachypnea: Satting in low ___ on RA. Ambulatory sats 
(___) notable for desat to high 70's. Has significant nail 
clubbing on exam, with ABG showing slightly increased A-a 
gradient, and TTE with late microbubbles consistent with 
hepatopulmonary syndrome. CXR with no effusion, CTA chest 
showing
clear lungs with bibasilar atelectasis(no PE). Ambulatory sats 
were checked again prior to discharge and he tolerated 
ambulation with a 93% saturation, so home oxygen was deferred.
[] Hepatology f/u as above

# HFpEF: Last echo ___ with EF 65%. No ___ edema noted this 
admission satting in the low 90's on room air although 
tachypneic. Continued on home Lasix 40 mg PO and 100 of 
aldactone po.

# Insomnia
#Anxiety: Acute on chronic anxiety in the setting of withdrawal 
and hospitalization. Was given Hydroxyzine 25 mg q6h prn and 
clonidine 0.1 mg po tid prn and continued on home trazodone 50 
mg qhs prn. Clonidine was continued on discharge as patient said 
that this medication had been helpful in the past.

# Diplopia/Visual disturbance
During this admission, he initially described blurry vision 
which he clarified as being monocular diplopia. There was one 
report of strabismus in the MICU but no subsequent episodes. no 
nystagmus and low concern for Wernicke's encephalopathy given 
that he had already undergone thiamine and folate loading. His 
monocular diplopia was worse on end-gaze, inconsistent on exam. 
This monocular diplopia self-resolved. He also complained of 
seeing small black dots, but no acute disturbances concerning 
for retinal detachment. His dots did not move with head 
movement, and were mostly at the periphery of his vision.
[] Ophthalmology f/u as outpatient

# Pancytopenia: Hgb 9.4, WBC 3.6, Plt 44. HIV and HCV negative. 
Most likely secondary to his longstanding alcohol abuse as well 
as his cirrhosis with splenomegaly. He did not require 
transfusions this admission.

# Coagulopathy: Coagulopathy secondary to cirrhosis, with
thrombocytopenia, INR 1.2. He did not have any acute bleeding 
episodes this admission.

# Opiate use disorder: His home ___ was initially held but

addiction social work team was consulted and assited in patient

Discharge Instructions:
Dear Mr. ___,

It was a pleasure taking care of you while you were in the 
hospital.

Why were you hospitalized?
- You were hospitalized for management of alcohol withdrawal.

What happened while you were hospitalized?
-You were treated for alcohol withdrawal with a 7 day 
phenobarbital taper.
-You were found to have altered mental status due to your liver 
disease, and were given lactulose, which causes diarrhea, in 
order to help improve your altered mental status.
-You were found to have low oxygen saturations and underwent an 
echocardiogram (ultrasound of your heart) that showed that you 
have hepatopulmonary syndrome, which is a condition where your 
lungs do not oxygenate your blood sufficiently because of your 
cirrhosis.

What should you do when discharged from the hospital? 
-Please take all medications as prescribed
-Please attend all outpatient appointments as scheduled.
-Please abstain from alcohol.

COMPARISON:  CT abdomen pelvis dated ___ and ___.

FINDINGS: 

LOWER CHEST: Focal opacity in the dependent aspect of the right lower lobe
(series 2, image 4) likely reflects atelectasis.  Dependent atelectasis is
also seen in the left lower lobe.  No pleural effusion or pericardial
effusion.

ABDOMEN:

HEPATOBILIARY: The liver demonstrate cirrhotic morphology.  Within the
limitation of a single phase study, no focal hepatic lesion.  There is no
evidence of intrahepatic or extrahepatic biliary dilatation.  The gallbladder
is within normal limits.  No ascites.

PANCREAS: The pancreas has normal attenuation throughout, without evidence of
focal lesions or pancreatic ductal dilatation.  There is no peripancreatic
stranding.

SPLEEN: The spleen measures 18.3 cm without focal lesion.

ADRENALS: The right and left adrenal glands are normal in size and shape.

URINARY: The kidneys are of normal and symmetric size with normal nephrogram. 
There is no evidence of focal renal lesions or hydronephrosis.  There is no
perinephric abnormality.

GASTROINTESTINAL: The stomach is unremarkable.  Small bowel loops demonstrate
normal caliber, wall thickness, and enhancement throughout.  The colon and
rectum are within normal limits.  The appendix is not visualized but no
secondary signs of appendicitis.

PELVIS: The urinary bladder and distal ureters are unremarkable.  There is no
free fluid in the pelvis.

REPRODUCTIVE ORGANS: The prostate and seminal vesicles are unremarkable.

LYMPH NODES: There are scattered prominent porta hepatic lymph node measuring
up to 0.8 cm (Series 2, image 34), unchanged.  Otherwise no retroperitoneal or
mesenteric lymphadenopathy.  There is no pelvic or inguinal lymphadenopathy.

is noted.  The portal venous system is patent.  There is a recanalized
paraumbilical vein with portosystemic collaterals in the ventral abdomen. 
There are perisplenic varices and splenorenal shunt (series 2, image 37). 
Celiac artery and its branches are patent.  The SMA and ___ are patent.

BONES: There is no evidence of worrisome osseous lesions or acute fracture. 
Left parasymphyseal sclerotic focus likely reflects a bone island.  Mild
compression deformities of T7 and T9 vertebral bodies are unchanged.

SOFT TISSUES: The abdominal and pelvic wall is within normal limits.

2. Cirrhotic liver with findings of portal hypertension including splenomegaly
and portosystemic collaterals.  No focal hepatic lesion identified given the
limitation of a single phase study.
